title: What not to put on the site for a restaurant group
metaTitle: What to leave off a restaurant group site
excerpt: Cut the logo animation. Keep the room, one dish, and a way to the menu or a table. A shorter site that tells the truth beats one that performs taste for its own team.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a toast that still needs a place, a time, and a way to sit down.
caption: Cups raised, and no restaurant named yet. The site still has to say where to sit. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should we remove first?
faqs.answer: The logo animation or any film that plays before the room and the dish. It reassures the team and tells a guest nothing about tonight. Replace it with one open restaurant, the hours, and a way to see the menu or book a table.

faqs.question: Should we delete the story and the press page?
faqs.answer: Move them below the restaurants, or remove them from the header if they are stale. A story that never helps a guest choose a door, and a press wall with no room attached, perform taste. Keep a true credit on the restaurant it belongs to.

faqs.question: Is a shorter site a problem?
faqs.answer: A shorter site with a clear purpose is easier to trust than a long one written to look like a group. Guests need the room, the dish, the hours, and the booking. Pages that exist only to sound complete can go.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The restaurant group website mistakes that waste a hungry guest's time are usually there to perform taste. A logo animation reassures the team and confuses someone deciding where to go tonight. Keep the room and one dish, and a clear way to see the menu or book a table.

A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs the idea of a restaurant group. Cut first. Add only what helps the next guest sit down.

## The logo animation

Start here, because it occupies the first seconds. A monogram draws itself. A film of hands and steam plays with no restaurant name. The workshop likes it. It looks like a launch. The guest learns nothing they can use: not which room, not the hours, not whether a table exists.

Replace it with one open restaurant, a photograph of the room or one dish, the hours, and the two actions. Menu. Book a table. Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is plain about the first 10 seconds. That is the window a clear value proposition has to earn a longer look. An intro spends the window on the mark.

If you love the film, mute it and move it below the facts, with a caption that names the room. If the film cannot say which restaurant it is, it is not ready. Autoplay sound is the same mistake with speakers. A guest on a bus will leave rather than hunt for mute.

The animation also hides whether the page is fast. Heavy intros arrive late. The guest needed hours. They got a drawing. Cut it before you debate the typeface.

## Pages that perform a group

Some pages exist so the site feels complete in a brand review. They are weak for a guest with an evening to plan.

A manifesto about gathering. A timeline of leases. A map of pins with no names. A grid called Explore. A stock skyline of the city. An untitled mosaic of plates. A journal that has not moved in a year, still in the header.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the site has a primary purpose for people who might come to you directly. The purpose is to help a guest pick a room and move toward a menu or a table. Pages that would not help that person, if they arrived hungry, are candidates to unpublish.

A story can stay when it helps a guest tell the rooms apart. A press page can stay as a list attached to the restaurants that earned it. A logo wall at the top of the homepage is the animation in type. The guest still needs the dish.

## What a shorter site keeps

After the cut, the site can be small and still complete.

- A homepage that leads with one open room, a dish, hours, menu, and book.
- Each restaurant, with its own facts and its own links.
- Menus a phone can read, with prices.
- Private dining, only if you sell it, with the minimum and a short note.
- A line on who cooks, linked onward, not a novel.
- Hours and addresses as text someone on the floor can change.

That set can be a handful of templates. You do not need a custom film for every season. You need the photographs, the sentences, and a Tuesday edit when lunch ends.

Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for pages that put a real subject first. Hanabi designs and builds marketing sites in that spirit: the room before the mark, and words you can correct without a new campaign. Bring the pages you suspect are theater. The cut is the work. The studio will not invent a waitlist or a headcount you do not have.

Shorter is easier to keep true. A long site drifts. A short one can be read by the operator before service. Truth is a maintenance problem as much as a writing problem.

## The room, the dish, the next step

Whatever you remove, these stay on the first screen and on each restaurant. The room. One dish. A way to the menu or a table. Hours in text, because a beautiful room on a closed Monday is a mistake you can prevent.

Check every remaining page against that set. A story page that never links to a booking has drifted. A menu that is a PDF nobody tested has drifted. A private dining page with ten fields and no minimum has drifted. Add the missing fact as a sentence and a link, not as a new campaign.

Use stable labels. Menu. Book a table. Variations are how the cut gets undone, because each variation seems to need its own landing page. One pair of labels. One destination per room.

Keep the type readable and the images sized for a phone. A short site that is slow, or that hides the hours under a desktop crop, still performs taste. The cut is not only pages. It is also the hero that says nothing.

## PDFs, music, and maps that fail

A few extras feel helpful and still belong on the list. A menu PDF that does not open on the phone. Music that plays. A map tile that is the only address. A popup that asks for an email before the hours. A single Book button that forgets which restaurant the guest chose.

Each one gives the office a sensation of completeness. The guest gets a stuck file, a surprise soundtrack, or the wrong book. Remove the audio. Put the address in text. Put the menu in the page. Aim the button at the room.

Unlabeled photographs are in this group. A plate with no restaurant name asks the guest to guess the door. If the dish is shared, say so. If it is not, label it. Discretion about a private party is not the same as a homepage with no nouns.

Inconsistent facts are the costliest. The header says one room is open, the menu is last winter's, and the widget offers a Monday. Pick the floor's truth and delete the synonyms. A shorter set of facts is easier to trust at 7 p.m.

## A cut list for this week

Print the sitemap. Mark each item keep, move, or drop.

Drop the logo animation, the autoplay sound, the stock skyline, the empty Explore page, and any form field that is not needed to book a table or ask about a private room.

Move press under the restaurants, the long story out of the header if it does not help a guest choose, and the group manifesto into one sentence or off the site.

Keep the rooms you can name, the menus you can update, the hours that match the door, and the booking links that remember the venue.

Then load the homepage on a phone at dinner time. If it still requires the animation to make sense, you have not replaced it. Put the room back before you restyle the footer.

Share the list before you delete. Someone will defend a page. Ask which guest decision it changes. If they cannot name the decision, the page can go. If they can, rewrite it until that decision is the heading, in the same week, before the old link returns in the footer.

Walk the kept pages with a host who worked last night. Ask them to find a closed day, a dish that is actually on, and the private room minimum, using only the phone. Every place they hesitate is still a mistake, even if it is not on the sitemap as its own URL. A hero that crops the room into a texture is a mistake. A button that books the flagship from the quiet room's page is a mistake. Write those down beside the dropped pages and fix them in the same pass. A cut list that only deletes URLs and leaves the wrong button will feel like a redesign and still send guests to the wrong door. The truth is the room, the dish, the hours, and the link. If those four agree, the site can be short. If they disagree, length will not save it. Do not add a page to explain a contradiction. Remove the contradiction. Then stop. The guest tonight does not need the site to be impressive. They need it to be usable before the kitchen closes. If the office wants one more thing on the homepage after the cut, make them name the guest decision it changes. A new film, a new award, or a new adjective that does not change the door, the dish, or the hours waits. The shorter page is the one you can still correct on a busy Thursday, when the only person free is the manager and the only tool they should need is a sentence.

## A different door, the same standard

The standard travels. A guest choosing a hotel for the night is as impatient as a guest choosing dinner, and just as likely to be on a phone. The facts change. The refusal of an empty introduction does not.

If the next site on your desk is a place to sleep, read [what the homepage has to prove for an independent hotel](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-an-independent-hotel). The first screen there has its own job. The cut you just made, animation off and facts on, is the habit to carry into that page.
